lead: Huffman coding and arithmetic coding are entropy coders. They turn a stream of symbols into bits, giving short code words to likely symbols and long code words to rare ones. Huffman coding builds an optimal prefix code from a tree. Arithmetic coding keeps a whole message inside one shrinking interval and writes a fraction from that interval. Run-length coding is a simple repeat-collapsing coder that replaces repeated values by a count; it is often used before an entropy coder. Huffman and arithmetic coding sit after quantization in an image compressor, and run-length coding often prepares data for them. A fax page, a palette image and a JPEG block all use one of them. The aim is to approach the entropy H, the theoretical minimum bits per symbol.
prereq: You need: 3.7 for entropy and bits per pixel.

sections.h3: Huffman coding: merge the two lowest probabilities

blocks.text: Huffman coding gives short code words to likely symbols. A prefix code is a set of code words in which no code word is the start of another. That property lets a decoder read bits one by one and stop as soon as a complete code word appears.

items: Make one leaf for each symbol, labelled with its probability pᵢ.
Put all nodes in a list.
Repeatedly remove the two nodes with the smallest probabilities and join them under a parent whose probability is their sum.
Stop when one root remains; label one child edge 0 and the other 1.
Read each symbol's code from root to leaf.
To decode, start at the root; for each bit go left on 0 or right on 1; at a leaf output the symbol and return to the root.

blocks.where: L is the average length in bits per symbol; pᵢ is the probability of symbol i; lᵢ is the length in bits of its code word.
H is the entropy in bits per symbol; log₂ is the base-2 logarithm; Σ runs over all symbols.

blocks.text: Every Huffman code has L ≥ H. Huffman is optimal among prefix codes, and L < H + 1. Two limits matter. With exactly two symbols, both code words must be 1 bit long, so L = 1 even when H is small (for p = 0.9 and 0.1, H ≈ 0.469 but L = 1). With more symbols the code words take different lengths and L can be larger than 1. The code table or the tree must be sent once, and that overhead matters for short messages.

sections.h3: Arithmetic coding: one interval for the whole message

blocks.text: Arithmetic coding does not give one code word per symbol. It represents the whole message by a number in [0, 1). Start with low = 0 and high = 1. For each symbol, take its cumulative lower bound cᵢ and probability pᵢ. The new interval is [low + (high − low)cᵢ, low + (high − low)(cᵢ + pᵢ)). After the last symbol, any number inside the final interval identifies the message, but the decoder needs to know when to stop. The encoder writes enough bits of such a number and also sends the message length, or uses a special end-of-message symbol, so the decoder stops after the right number of symbols.

The decoder mirrors the encoder. It starts with [0, 1), finds which symbol's subinterval contains the received number, outputs that symbol, then maps the number into that subinterval and repeats. It stops when it has output the sent message length, or when it outputs the end-of-message symbol. For skewed probabilities arithmetic coding beats Huffman over long messages. In a long message with p = 0.9, arithmetic coding spends about −log₂ 0.9 = 0.152 bits per occurrence of that symbol on average, against a full 1 bit for Huffman. A single short message still costs whole bits plus a termination cost. Finite precision limits the interval size; practical coders renormalize and emit bits as they go.

sections.h3: Run-length coding: turn repeats into count pairs

blocks.text: Run-length coding (RLE) replaces each run by a pair (value, length). A run is a maximal sequence of equal values. Encoding: scan left to right; start a count at 1; add 1 while the next value is the same; when the value changes, write the pair and start a new count; write the last pair. Decoding: read a pair (v, l), write v exactly l times, then read the next pair.

For binary and palette images, long runs of the same value are common, so RLE is simple and fast. For a noisy photograph, neighbouring pixels rarely repeat, so most runs have length 1 and the count adds overhead; the file can grow.

spec.aria: A Huffman tree: root 1.0 splits into leaf a 0.4 and node 0.6; 0.6 splits into leaf d 0.2 and node 0.4; 0.4 splits into leaves b and c, 0.2 each. Left edges are 0, right edges 1. A table gives the codes, and the row 0000111000 is shown as the pairs (0,4) (1,3) (0,3).

examples.question: Four symbols have probabilities a = 0.4, b = 0.2, c = 0.2, d = 0.2. Build the Huffman tree, give each code, compute average length L and entropy H, and encode the bit row 0000111000 with run-length coding. State whether the Huffman code is within 0.1 bit of H.
steps: Start with four leaves: a = 0.4, b = 0.2, c = 0.2, d = 0.2.
Merge the two lowest probabilities, b and c: b + c = 0.4. The list is now a = 0.4, d = 0.2, and the pair node 0.4.
Merge the two lowest probabilities, d and the pair node: d + 0.4 = 0.6. The list is now a = 0.4 and 0.6.
Merge a and 0.6: 0.4 + 0.6 = 1.0. This is the root.
Read codes with left edge 0 and right edge 1: a = 0, d = 10, b = 110, c = 111.
The code lengths are l(a) = 1, l(d) = 2, l(b) = 3, l(c) = 3 bits.
The gap is L − H = 2.0 − 1.92 = 0.08 bit, which is within 0.1 bit.
examples.answer: The Huffman codes are a = 0, d = 10, b = 110, c = 111; L = 2.0 bits per symbol, H ≈ 1.92 bits per symbol, a gap of 0.08 bit; the row encodes as (0,4)(1,3)(0,3), 3 pairs.
examples.check:
import math
p = {'a': 0.4, 'b': 0.2, 'c': 0.2, 'd': 0.2}
codes = {'a': '0', 'd': '10', 'b': '110', 'c': '111'}
L = sum(p[s] * len(codes[s]) for s in p)
H = -sum(pi * math.log2(pi) for pi in p.values())
row = '0000111000'
runs = []
cur = row[0]
count = 1
for ch in row[1:]:
    if ch == cur:
        count += 1
    else:
        runs.append((cur, count))
        cur = ch
        count = 1
runs.append((cur, count))
print(L)
print(round(H, 2))
print(round(L - H, 2))
print(len(runs))

traps: Merging the two highest probabilities gives a valid tree but not a minimum-length Huffman code; always merge the two lowest.
A code such as a = 0, b = 01 is not prefix-free because 0 is a prefix of 01; codes must sit only at leaves.
Average length weights each code length by its probability pᵢ, not by how many symbols have that length.
Run-length coding is not automatically smaller; a noisy photograph has short runs, so the count pairs add overhead.
The Huffman tree or code table is part of the compressed data, so ignore it only when the decoder already knows it.

quiz.q: State the prefix property of a Huffman code.
quiz.a: No code word is a prefix of another code word, so the decoder can stop at the first complete code word.

quiz.q: Why can a Huffman code have L greater than H even when the tree is built correctly?
quiz.a: Huffman code lengths are whole numbers of bits, but H can be fractional. The code must round each length up or down, so L is at least H and can be up to nearly 1 bit larger.

quiz.q: Symbols x, y, z have probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.25. Build a Huffman code and compute L.

quiz.a: Write 1 five times: 11111. Write 0 two times: 00. Write 1 three times: 111. The decoded row is 1111100111.

quiz.q: A source has two symbols with probabilities 0.9 and 0.1. Compare Huffman L with H and explain why arithmetic coding is better here.
quiz.a: Huffman must give one code word of 1 bit to each symbol, so L = 1 bit. H = −0.9 log₂ 0.9 − 0.1 log₂ 0.1 ≈ 0.469 bits. In a long message, arithmetic coding spends about −log₂ 0.9 = 0.152 bits per occurrence of the likely symbol on average, against 1 bit for Huffman, so it approaches H and saves more than 0.5 bit per symbol on average. A short message still costs whole bits plus a termination cost.

quiz.q: What must be sent with Huffman-coded data so the decoder can recover the symbols?
quiz.a: The decoder needs the code table or the Huffman tree, including which symbol belongs to each code, unless that table is fixed in advance.

quiz.q: A 512 × 512 binary image is mostly white with long runs. Would run-length coding or Huffman coding alone suit it better? Explain.
quiz.a: Run-length coding suits it better because long runs of white or black become few (value, length) pairs. Huffman coding alone still codes every pixel and does not collapse runs. In practice the two can be combined.

quiz.q: What does a run-length pair (v, l) mean?
quiz.a: The value v is repeated l times in the decoded row.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical image and video codecs use arithmetic-like range coding or asymmetric numeral systems instead of plain Huffman, because they follow skewed probabilities more closely. Context-adaptive methods change probabilities from block to block, and some standards combine run-length coding with entropy coding. Search next for range coding, context-adaptive binary arithmetic coding, and JPEG XL or HEVC entropy coding.
